intro: The shortest of the six songs pictures friends drinking and writing verses in a porcelain pavilion, then the same scene upside down in the pond. This is the third song of one live 1939 Amsterdam performance of the whole work, so the singers and orchestra continue across the set.
question: How can a three-minute song be both a scene and its own mirror image?

sections.label: A′ · Tempo I — the return
sections.mNote: pavilion words return abbreviated, ending in a held ppp chord

cues.title: Winds before voices
cues.text: Von der Jugend (“Of Youth”) marks itself Behaglich heiter — comfortably cheerful. For its first half-minute no strings play: a held horn note, faint triangle strokes, and flutes, oboe and clarinets trading trilling figures.
cues.evidence: In the first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; IMSLP #20582, printed pp. 51–52) the strings first play at rehearsal figure 2, with the tenor; before it only winds, one horn and triangle sound. The recording opens near −30 dB and rises to about −17 dB by 0:10.

cues.title: The tenor and the pavilion
cues.text: The tenor enters with “Mitten in dem kleinen Teiche” — in the middle of the little pond — over light, bouncing strings (saltando). The tune leans on a five-note pentatonic scale, the cycle’s most obvious touch of chinoiserie; the pavilion is “of green and white porcelain”.
cues.evidence: The score puts the tenor’s entry at rehearsal figure 2, with saltando strings; the Mahler Foundation page for this song calls it the cycle’s most obviously pentatonic movement. The recording’s level rises to about −10 dB around 0:25–0:35, and 0:30 is among its five loudest 5-second windows; no exact entry time is claimed.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Swing to G major
cues.text: Around 0:50 the music leaves B♭ major for G major, a third lower. Clarinets and bassoons chatter, a muted trumpet calls, and the tenor returns with “In dem Häuschen sitzen Freunde” — friends sit in the little house, drinking and chatting.
cues.evidence: A strong boundary in the report is 0:50 (novelty 0.93), where the local key estimate changes from B♭ major (0:15–0:45) to G major (0:50–1:15). The score changes key signature at rehearsal figure 5, and a muted trumpet is marked there.

cues.title: A pavilion that never stood
cues.text: The porcelain pavilion probably began as a misreading. The Chinese poem usually named as source, Li Bai’s “Banquet at Tao’s Pavilion”, names the Tao family in its title; Judith Gautier’s French version turned the character into “porcelain”, and Bethge and Mahler kept it. The identification has been questioned.
cues.evidence: Mahler Archives, Von der Jugend page (http://www.mahlerarchives.net/Archive%20documents/DLvDE/Der_Jugend.htm), and Peter Laki’s note for the Cleveland Orchestra, movement 3 paragraph (https://www.clevelandorchestra.com/works/das-lied-von-der-erde), describe the Gautier misreading; Edwin K. C. Li, JRMA 150/2 (2025), fn 3 and 8, lists the Li Bai poem as the generally agreed source and notes Liao Fushu’s doubts about Qian Renkang’s identification.

cues.title: Ruhiger: the still pond
cues.text: Around 1:42 the pace eases (Ruhiger, “calmer”) and the harmony darkens to G minor. A solo violin sings above hushed strings while the tenor describes the little pond’s still surface, where everything “shows itself strangely” as a reflection.
cues.evidence: Novelty peaks at 1:40 (0.89) and 1:44 (0.96) follow the loudest stretch near 1:20 (−5 dB); local key estimates read G minor from 1:40. The score marks Ruhiger at rehearsal figure 10 over a solo violin line.

cues.title: The mirror slows
cues.text: The marking becomes Langsam (slowly) and the line stretches towards a near-halt, with Poco rit. and Rit. molto written in. One of the song’s quietest windows falls around here, just before the first tempo snaps back.
cues.evidence: A strong boundary at 2:06 (0.87) and the strongest of all at 2:20 (1.00); 2:25 is among the five quietest windows. The score places Langsam at figure 11 and the rit. at figure 12.

cues.title: Toblach, summer 1908
cues.text: Mahler composed the songs largely in summer 1908, forbidden the long walks he needed for composing. From Bethge’s 83 paraphrases of 38 poets he picked seven poems; a gentle scene like this sits among songs of wine, autumn and farewell. In September he told Bruno Walter he had been very diligent.
cues.evidence: Stephen E. Hefling’s work introduction for Universal Edition: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Works/Das-Lied-von-der-Erde/P0109538 (doctors’ restrictions, 83 paraphrases of 38 poets, seven selected, letters to Walter of July and September 1908).

cues.title: Tempo I subito: upside down
cues.text: Tempo I subito: the first speed returns at once, the strings’ mutes come off, and the tenor repeats the pavilion words — “Alles auf dem Kopfe stehend”, everything standing on its head — then the bridge as an inverted half-moon.
cues.evidence: A boundary at 2:44 (0.81) with the level climbing from about −19 dB to −10 dB by 2:55. The score marks Tempo I subito at figure 14 with Dämpfer ab for the strings.

cues.title: Held notes fade
cues.text: In the last bars the winds and strings dim to ppp under a fermata. Listen to the final chord die away; the level falls by about fourteen decibels in ten seconds and the recording ends in near-silence.
cues.evidence: Relative level falls from −28 dB at 3:15 to −42 dB at 3:25, the quietest windows of the file. The score ends with ppp and a fermata.

transitions.title: B♭ major gives way to G major
transitions.how: The pavilion music ends and the key signature at rehearsal figure 5 changes to G major, a minor third below the B♭ home key. A short orchestral link carries the move: clarinets repeat chattering chords, bassoons trill, a muted trumpet calls, and the triangle keeps a soft shimmer. The tenor’s next words, about the friends in the house, arrive only at figure 6, so the new key is heard first without any voice.
transitions.evidence: Novelty peak 0:50 (0.93) and the local key estimate moving from B♭ major to G major at 0:50. The signature change, clarinet figure and muted trumpet are read from the 1912 full score (IMSLP #20582, printed pp. 52–53).

transitions.title: A solo violin leads into Ruhiger
transitions.how: The G-major friends’ music rises to the song’s loudest stretch, then falls away over a solo violin line. At Ruhiger (“calmer”) the same tonic G turns minor, the strings play softly in a gently rocking figure, and the violin keeps singing above the tenor. The change is one of mode, tempo and weight rather than a new key centre: the scene is the same, now seen on the surface of the water.
transitions.evidence: The loudest windows are 1:00–1:20 and the strongest boundaries follow at 1:40 (0.89) and 1:44 (0.96), where the local key estimate reads G minor. Ruhiger and the solo violin are marked in the score at figure 10 (printed p. 57).

transitions.title: Almost stopping, then the first tempo
transitions.how: Mahler slows the reflection in stages: Langsam, then Poco rit. and Rit. molto, a short return to a moderate tempo, and a last Rit. and Molto rit. that leave the music almost still. Then comes Tempo I subito: the first speed at once, the mutes off the strings and B♭ major back in place. The tenor sings the pavilion words again, so the song closes the circle it opened.
transitions.evidence: The quietest windows include 2:25, a boundary at 2:44 (0.81) follows, and the level climbs from about −19 dB to −10 dB by 2:55. The sequence of markings is read from printed pp. 58–59 of the 1912 full score.

source.title: Mahler, Das Lied von der Erde, III. Von der Jugend, full score (Universal Edition, 1912, plate U.E. 3637)
source.locator: IMSLP #20582; printed pp. 51–60. Entry times are proportioned between the audio boundaries at 0:50, 1:42, 2:06 and 2:44 and are approximate; which edition the 1939 orchestra used is not documented.

timeline.note: A held horn note and faint triangle strokes open the song.
Second flute and oboe weave a five-note figure over the horn.
Piccolo, flutes and clarinets trade trilling figures; bassoons answer low.
The tenor enters over saltando violins and violas.
In G major, clarinets and bassoons chatter, a muted trumpet calls and the triangle shimmers.
Violins and violas play near the fingerboard under the tenor’s words about the friends.
A solo violin rises above the full chamber-weight orchestra at the song’s loudest point.
Ruhiger: hushed strings, a rocking figure, and the solo violin above the tenor.
Langsam: the tenor sings of the mirror image while winds sustain and the basses pluck.
Tempo I subito: mutes off, the tenor repeats the pavilion words above bouncing strings.
Winds and violins dim to a held ppp chord.

fields.note: The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Kerstin Thorborg does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain.
fields.note: A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established.
fields.note: Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony anticipates Mahler’s so closely that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony. The cantata Das klagende Lied, written at eighteen and nineteen, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881, and Mahler turned to the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
